latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Insufficient macrophage, T-cell, CD4, Th1/IFN-gamma, and granulomatous containment of inhaled or latent Cryptococcus. This activity is raised by advanced HIV, solid organ transplantation, corticosteroids, TNF inhibitors, hematologic malignancy, cirrhosis, renal failure, diabetes, and idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pulmonary acquisition or latent pulmonary reactivation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inhaled Cryptococcus neoformans or C. gattii establishes pulmonary infection or reactivates from a latent pulmonary focus. This is the usual gateway for later bloodstream and CNS dissemination.
Total viable encapsulated yeast burden across lung, blood, CSF, and seeded tissues. Drives cryptococcal antigen burden, culture positivity, tissue invasion, and antifungal response kinetics.

Bloodstream spread from pulmonary or tissue focus to CNS, skin, soft tissue, bone, lymph nodes, prostate, eye, or other sterile compartments. Cryptococcemia itself defines disseminated disease and predicts high burden.

Cryptococcus crosses into leptomeninges, perivascular spaces, ventricles, or brain parenchyma, producing meningitis, meningoencephalitis, cranial neuropathies, hearing loss, altered mental status, seizures, hydrocephalus, and persistent CSF culture or antigen positivity.

Capsular polysaccharide, yeast burden, impaired CSF resorption, hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, or cryptococcoma raise intracranial pressure. ICP can be normal in transplant or atypical cases, but when high it strongly drives headache, vomiting, cranial neuropathy, vision/hearing injury, and mortality.

Pulmonary nodules, masses, consolidation, cavitation, lymphadenopathy, diffuse infiltrates, or respiratory failure caused by lung cryptococcosis. It can mimic tuberculosis, malignancy, bacterial pneumonia, or other fungal pneumonia.

Hematogenous seeding or less commonly direct inoculation of skin, fascia, or soft tissue, producing papules, nodules, ulcers, cellulitis-like lesions, purpura, soft-tissue abscess, or rare necrotizing fasciitis-like disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic inflammatory and organ dysfunction response
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Host inflammatory response and organ dysfunction from disseminated cryptococcal burden, fungemia, CNS disease, pulmonary failure, soft-tissue dissemination, coinfection, delayed antifungal therapy, or immune reconstitution.

Delayed active therapy, absent amphotericin-flucytosine induction in high-burden disease, flucytosine unavailability or toxicity, poor azole susceptibility, inadequate CNS penetration, renal dose interruption, or adherence failure sustaining viable cryptococcal burden.

Exaggerated inflammatory worsening after ART initiation or immunosuppression reduction despite falling fungal burden. It can worsen meningitis, intracranial pressure, pulmonary lesions, lymph nodes, and skin lesions.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Defective cellular immunity permits inhaled or latent Cryptococcus to persist and expand in lung.
Pulmonary infection or reactivation generates viable encapsulated yeast burden.
Higher viable burden increases bloodstream invasion and multi-organ seeding.
Cryptococcus has marked CNS tropism after bloodstream spread.
CNS yeast and capsular polysaccharide impair CSF flow and resorption.
Skin and soft tissue lesions are common visible markers of disseminated cryptococcosis.
Pulmonary entry or reactivation produces nodules, infiltrates, cavitation, or diffuse lung disease.
Delayed, inactive, poorly penetrating, interrupted, or unavailable therapy lowers active antifungal coverage.
Insufficient active antifungal exposure sustains viable burden and slows CSF sterilization.
Serum cryptococcal antigen burden reflects capsular polysaccharide from invasive or disseminated disease.
CSF antigen rises with cryptococcal CNS burden.
Cryptococcemia is direct evidence of hematogenous dissemination.
Viable yeast in CSF produces positive CSF culture until sterilized by induction therapy.
Pulmonary cryptococcosis can yield Cryptococcus from sputum, BAL, or lung tissue when sampled.
Skin, fascia, or tissue biopsy/culture can reveal encapsulated yeast in cutaneous or soft tissue involvement.
Disseminated fungal burden and inflammatory response commonly cause fever, though it can be muted in transplant or steroid exposure.
Fever, pain, hypoxemia, shock physiology, or systemic stress raises heart rate.
Tissue invasive cryptococcosis can raise CRP, but the response can be low in immunosuppressed hosts.
WBC can be normal, high, or low depending on HIV, transplant drugs, steroids, bacterial coinfection, and marrow reserve.
Advanced HIV, immunosuppression, or hematologic disease often produces lymphopenia and weak cryptococcal containment.
Pulmonary cryptococcosis can present with cough or minimal respiratory symptoms.
Diffuse or severe pulmonary disease impairs gas exchange and causes dyspnea.
Severe lung involvement or ARDS-spectrum injury lowers oxygen saturation.
Pulmonary cryptococcosis commonly produces solitary or multiple nodules.
Cavitary nodules or excavated lesions occur and can mimic tuberculosis or malignancy.
Headache is the dominant symptom of cryptococcal meningitis.
Meningeal irritation may produce neck stiffness, though it is absent in many immunosuppressed patients.
CSF pleocytosis is typical but may be mild or absent in severely immunosuppressed hosts.
Meningeal inflammation commonly raises CSF protein.
Cryptococcal meningitis can lower CSF glucose, although values can remain normal.
CSF opening pressure directly measures clinically relevant ICP elevation.
Raised ICP commonly causes nausea and vomiting.
Raised ICP, meningoencephalitis, hydrocephalus, or shock can impair consciousness.
Cranial nerve or inner-ear involvement can produce hearing loss in cryptococcal meningitis.
CNS infection creates an event path that changes treatment penetration and ICP management needs.
Elevated ICP is a treatable, outcome-relevant complication of cryptococcal meningitis.
Disseminated disease can produce papular, pustular, nodular, ulcerative, or molluscum-like lesions.
Soft-tissue seeding can mimic cellulitis, abscess, or necrotizing fasciitis.
Necrotic, abscessed, or compartment-threatening soft-tissue cryptococcosis may require debridement or drainage.
High-burden disseminated cryptococcosis can present with sepsis-like shock, especially with soft-tissue disease or coinfection.
Shock, baseline renal disease, amphotericin exposure, and multi-organ failure raise AKI hazard.
Severe disseminated infection and shock can produce DIC physiology in rare severe presentations.
Severe pulmonary cryptococcosis can progress to respiratory failure or ARDS-spectrum injury.
Immune reconstitution after ART or immunosuppression reduction creates IRIS event risk.
Cryptococcal IRIS can worsen meningeal inflammation and intracranial pressure despite falling organism burden.
CNS disease is a central mortality driver in disseminated cryptococcosis.
Uncontrolled intracranial pressure causes neurologic death, herniation risk, and disability.
Shock, respiratory failure, AKI, DIC, and multi-organ failure raise lifespan hazard.
Delayed or inadequate fungicidal induction leaves high organism burden and worsens outcome.
Added during horizontal ontology audit: this axis is a real shared inflammatory/CNS involvement feature for this disease family, not a case-specific ranking patch.

axes.shape_free_text: Nonspecific systemic inflammatory marker that commonly rises in clinically significant pulmonary, metastatic, or disseminated infection; included through horizontal fairness audit.
Oral thrush is a structured host-context clue for advanced cellular immunodeficiency or Candida overgrowth; it is not a disease-specific mechanism for this leaf.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Higher opening pressure directly raises ICP complication risk.
Uncontrolled ICP raises acute mortality and neurologic injury risk.
CNS involvement worsens outcome even when other organ axes are modest.
Worsening oxygenation signals respiratory failure or ARDS-spectrum injury.
Respiratory failure is a major death path in disseminated cryptococcosis with lung involvement.
Shock and hypoperfusion raise AKI risk.
DIC physiology can produce hemorrhage in severe sepsis-like cryptococcosis.
Major bleeding or hemorrhagic shock raises mortality.

axis_couplings.conditionality: cryptococcal soft tissue necrosis, abscess, or fasciitis-like disease
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Adequate debridement or drainage lowers local soft-tissue burden.

axis_couplings.conditionality: ART initiation or immunosuppression reduction after cryptococcal disease
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Cryptococcal IRIS can worsen CNS inflammation and ICP.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rare reduced susceptibility or species-level concerns reduce polyene killing.
Baseline renal impairment or amphotericin nephrotoxicity constrains exposure and monitoring.

failure_modes: delayed initiation after high organism burden
renal toxicity or electrolyte wasting limiting exposure
lack of flucytosine companion drug in high-burden CNS disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid fungicidal pressure against disseminated, CNS, or severe pulmonary cryptococcosis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Unavailability, renal accumulation, or marrow toxicity removes the synergistic induction path.
Renal impairment increases flucytosine exposure and marrow toxicity unless dose-adjusted.

failure_modes: functional monotherapy if amphotericin is stopped early
treatments.context_specific_role: Companion drug that accelerates CSF and bloodstream sterilization when high-burden disseminated or CNS disease is present.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Reduced azole susceptibility, high MIC, or inadequate dose weakens consolidation.
Azole-only therapy is slow for high-burden CNS disease and should not replace fungicidal induction when induction is feasible.

treatments.context_specific_role: Longer-duration stepdown or suppressive antifungal pressure after induction or for lower-burden non-CNS contexts when appropriate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Therapeutic CSF removal acts through lowering pressure, not directly killing yeast.
Thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy increases LP or drain bleeding risk.

failure_modes: procedure contraindicated by mass lesion or coagulopathy

side_effects.interpretation: LP, lumbar drain, or shunt bleeding/infection risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Direct management of elevated ICP, a separate causal path from antifungal killing.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ART is causal only when HIV-driven immune failure is present.
Early immune restoration in active CNS cryptococcosis raises IRIS and ICP worsening risk.

failure_modes: uncontrolled fungal burden before immune restoration

side_effects.interpretation: cryptococcal IRIS risk during immune restoration

treatments.context_specific_role: Restores HIV-impaired host control while requiring timing against fungal burden and CNS inflammation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Lowering steroids, antimetabolites, or biologics can restore cryptococcal containment when clinically feasible.
Over-reduction can cause rejection or inflammatory worsening; drug interactions with azoles matter.

side_effects.interpretation: paradoxical inflammatory worsening after immune restoration

treatments.context_specific_role: Host-defense restoration in transplant, steroid, TNF inhibitor, or other iatrogenic immunosuppression contexts.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Procedural source control matters when necrotic tissue, abscess, compartment threat, or diagnostic tissue need is present.
Thrombocytopenia or DIC makes repeated debridement hazardous.

failure_modes: multifocal dissemination continues despite local control
diagnosis delayed as bacterial necrotizing fasciitis
treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical reduction of necrotic or abscessed cryptococcal soft-tissue burden and diagnostic tissue acquisition.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Respiratory support is useful when oxygenation or work of breathing is impaired.

side_effects.interpretation: secondary infection risk when invasive ventilation is required

treatments.context_specific_role: Bridge for hypoxemic respiratory failure while antifungal therapy acts.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluid supports perfusion when shock physiology or hypovolemia is present.

side_effects.interpretation: over-resuscitation can worsen pulmonary edema or ARDS

treatments.context_specific_role: Perfusion bridge for sepsis-like shock while antifungal and source-control paths act.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressor support is useful only when hypotension or shock physiology is present.

failure_modes: arrhythmia or ischemia at high dose

side_effects.interpretation: excess vasoconstriction can worsen ischemic injury at high doses

treatments.context_specific_role: Hemodynamic bridge for shock physiology while antifungal and source-control paths act.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: KRT supports severe AKI complications and changes antifungal dosing, but does not kill Cryptococcus.

failure_modes: altered amphotericin or flucytosine dosing requirements

side_effects.interpretation: dialysis catheter and anticoagulation bleeding risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Renal support for severe AKI, uremia, refractory electrolyte derangements, acidosis, or volume overload during disseminated cryptococcosis.

supportive_care: Document whether disease is disseminated by cryptococcemia or by involvement of two or more noncontiguous sites; keep blood, CSF, tissue, respiratory culture, antigen, PCR, and pathology as confirmatory/context evidence rather than ordinary presentation observations.

Assess host state explicitly: HIV status, CD4 count, viral load, transplant type and date, tacrolimus/cyclosporine/MMF exposure, corticosteroid or TNF inhibitor exposure, malignancy, cirrhosis, CKD, diabetes, pregnancy, and prior azole exposure.

For headache, vomiting, hearing change, cranial neuropathy, altered mental status, or disseminated disease, perform lumbar puncture when safe; record opening pressure, CSF cell count, glucose, protein, culture, and cryptococcal antigen.
Manage elevated ICP as its own causal path: repeat therapeutic lumbar punctures, lumbar drain, ventriculostomy, or shunt according to symptoms, opening pressure, hydrocephalus, and local expertise.

Image chest when pulmonary symptoms, hypoxemia, abnormal exam, or disseminated disease is present; cryptococcal nodules, cavitation, masses, lymphadenopathy, consolidation, and diffuse infiltrates can mimic TB, malignancy, or bacterial pneumonia.
Inspect skin and soft tissue for papules, nodules, ulcers, cellulitis, purpura, abscess, necrosis, or fasciitis-like disease; biopsy or culture suspicious lesions when safe.
Track temperature, MAP, oxygenation, mental status, urine output, creatinine, potassium, magnesium, CBC, platelets, ALT/AST, bilirubin, INR, and CRP during induction and critical illness.
Monitor amphotericin renal toxicity and electrolyte wasting closely; pre-hydration and electrolyte replacement may be needed, and lipid formulation reduces but does not remove nephrotoxicity.
Dose-adjust flucytosine for renal function and monitor drug exposure when available, CBC, hepatic enzymes, and gastrointestinal toxicity.
Use fluconazole or other azole stepdown/suppression with attention to susceptibility, CNS burden, drug interactions, QTc, liver enzymes, renal dosing, and adherence.
Coordinate ART timing in HIV-associated cryptococcosis to balance mortality benefit of immune restoration against cryptococcal IRIS and ICP worsening risk.
In transplant or autoimmune disease, coordinate immunosuppression reduction with transplant/rheumatology/oncology teams; monitor for rejection, flare, drug interactions, and inflammatory rebound.
For soft-tissue necrosis, abscess, compartment threat, or diagnostic uncertainty, involve surgery early for debridement, drainage, and tissue diagnosis while continuing systemic antifungal therapy.

Use sepsis organ support when shock occurs: balanced crystalloid, vasopressor to adequate perfusion, lactate reassessment, ventilation/oxygen support, renal support when indicated, and bleeding/DIC management.
Evaluate persistent symptoms or positive cultures for uncontrolled CNS pressure, inadequate antifungal exposure, drug toxicity limiting therapy, IRIS, new dissemination, or coinfection.

Consult infectious diseases for antifungal induction, consolidation, duration, susceptibility interpretation, ART/immunosuppression timing, and complication search; add neurology/neurosurgery, pulmonology, ophthalmology, surgery, nephrology, and transplant specialists according to involved axes.
